paper_title: D3D: Decoupled Diffusion Drafting for Asynchronous Speculative Decoding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Target-conditioned diffusion drafters predict candidate tokens in parallel, yet each new block must wait for updated target-model hidden states. This forces drafting and verification to run sequentially, limiting speedup even though each block is generated in one pass. We introduce D3D, a standalone diffusion drafter that removes this inter-round dependency. D3D combines blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision to achieve long accepted prefixes without target hidden states. This independence lets D3D draft successor blocks during verification in one packed pass, enabling asynchronous speculative decoding. We progressively prune layers according to their effect on acceptance length to reduce the cost of packed drafting. Removing five of 36 layers retains over 99\% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks with Qwen3-8B as the target. Across seven benchmarks, D3D averages 5.00$\times$ and 5.71$\times$ decoding speedup with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets, compared with 4.03$\times$ and 3.67$\times$ for DFlash. On GSM8K with Qwen3-32B, speedup reaches 7.48$\times$. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/fudan-generative-vision/D3D.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Autoregressive language models dominate open-ended text generation, but their inherently sequential decoding limits token-level parallelism. Generating one token at time leads to poor hardware utilization and high inference latency, especially in memory-bound settings. Speculative decoding alleviates this bottleneck by using lightweight draft model to propose multiple future tokens, which the target model then verifies in parallel [Stern et al., 2018, Xia et al., 2023, Leviathan et al., 2023, Chen et al., 2023, Kim et al., 2023, Miao et al., 2024]. With suitable acceptance rule, speculative decoding preserves the target distribution, yielding the same output distribution as standard decoding with the target model. The speedup achieved by speculative decoding depends on the number of accepted tokens, draft latency, and verification cost. Recent work has therefore focused on improving draft accuracy while keeping draft latency low. Many methods attach auxiliary predictors to the target model or condition separate drafter on intermediate representations from the target model [Cai et al., 2024, Ankner et al., 2024, Gloeckle et al., 2024, Li et al., 2024, 2025, Cheng et al., 2024, Xiao et al., 2024]. However, autoregressive and recurrent drafters still generate candidate tokens sequentially, causing draft latency to grow with the candidate length. Parallel drafting addresses the sequential generation cost by predicting multiple candidate positions simultaneously. PARD adapts pretrained autoregressive model into parallel drafter, while DiffuSpec and SpecDiff-2 use diffusion models to generate multiple candidate tokens concurrently [An et al., 2025, Li et al., 2026, Sandler et al., 2025]. PARD-2 further aligns training with acceptance length and supports both target-dependent and target-independent inference [An et al., 2026]. DART and DFlash improve draft 1 quality by conditioning parallel drafters on intermediate representations from the target model [Liu et al., 2026, Chen et al., 2026]. In particular, DFlash uses block diffusion model to generate an entire candidate block in single forward pass. Recent methods improve target-conditioned parallel drafts by enriching target-feature fusion [Zhang et al., 2026a], refining block predictions with causal context [Huang et al., 2026, Rheinboldt et al., 2026, Zheng and Li, 2026], and weighting training positions according to their contribution to acceptance [Wu et al., 2026]. Target-conditioned parallel heads have also been used to generate causal draft trees [Hu et al., 2026]. In these implementations, the next draft block requires updated target-model representations. For diffusion drafter that generates an entire candidate block in single forward pass, drafting latency still depends on the drafters depth. Recent work reports log-linear relationship between decoder depth and acceptance rate for shallow autoregressive drafters [Yan et al., 2025b]. Larger drafters can improve acceptance, but typically require more time to generate each candidate block. When drafting and verification execute sequentially, this additional draft latency can offset the benefit of accepting more tokens. This creates trade-off between draft quality and draft latency. Beyond the cost of each forward pass, conditioning on fresh target-model representations creates an execution dependency between drafting rounds. In DFlash, verification produces representations of newly accepted tokens that the drafter consumes in the next round [Chen et al., 2026]. The next draft must therefore wait for these representations, even though the drafter predicts all positions within block in parallel. Inspired by Speculative Speculative Decoding (SSD), we prepare drafts for possible verification outcomes while the target verifies the current block [Kumar et al., 2026]. SSD demonstrates this approach with autoregressive drafters that generate candidate sequences through multiple sequential steps. We use standalone diffusion drafter to predict each candidate block from its conditioning prefix in single forward pass. The modeling challenge is to obtain long accepted prefixes without target hidden states while keeping drafting fast enough to complete within the verification interval. We introduce D3D, decoupled diffusion drafter built around target-aligned training and progressive layer pruning. Our contributions are as follows: 1. Target-aligned standalone diffusion drafting. We combine blockwise denoising and auxiliary autoregressive supervision on target-generated responses to train standalone, single-pass drafter from pretrained weights. At block size 16, D3D exceeds every baseline in acceptance length on each of the seven benchmarks for both targets, averaging 7.88 with Qwen3-8B and 7.73 with Qwen3-32B  (Table 1)  . 2. Pruning redundant drafter layers. We remove layers with the smallest effect on validation acceptance length, with recovery training between removals. With Qwen3-8B as the target, removing five of 36 layers (13.9%) retains over 99% of mean acceptance length and raises mean speedup from 4.44 to 4.69 across three benchmarks (Figure 2). 3. Asynchronous speculative decoding. During target verification, D3D prepares possible successor blocks in one packed drafter pass and reuses matching block in the next round. Across seven benchmarks, it achieves the highest mean decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding among the evaluated methods: 5.00 with Qwen3-8B and 5.71 with Qwen3-32B  (Table 1)  .

sections.title: 2.1 Parallel and Diffusion Drafting
sections.content: PARD adapts an autoregressive backbone for masked parallel prediction [An et al., 2025]. PARD-2 uses causal masked-token prediction and stochastically injects target features during training, allowing the same 2 drafter to operate with or without these features at inference [An et al., 2026]. DFlash injects projected target features into the attention keys and values of each diffusion layer [Chen et al., 2026]. D2SD retains this conditioning in both its initial drafter and its second drafter, which generates continuations from variable-length prefixes [Zhang et al., 2026b]. D2SD jointly verifies these alternative continuations in the current round. D3D prepares successor blocks for possible next-round prefixes while the target verifies the current block. DeLS-Spec independently trains short-context predictor and combines its logits with those of frozen DFlash backbone [Zheng and Li, 2026]. Its decoupling separates component training, while the backbone continues to consume target features. D3D shares target-independent inference with PARD and PARD-2, and learns its own prefix representations through diffusion and autoregressive supervision on target-generated responses. Its masked blocks use bidirectional attention, and training does not inject target hidden states. For D3D, we further prune layers based on their measured effect on acceptance length. SpecDiff-2 derives streak distillation from surrogate for the expected accepted prefix length [Sandler et al., 2025]. PARD-2 weights token losses using the cumulative product of the target models confidence in preceding tokens [An et al., 2026]. D-PACE derives example-dependent position weights from surrogate for expected accepted length [Wu et al., 2026]. DFlash uses exponentially decaying position weights to emphasize early predictions [Chen et al., 2026]. We retain DFlashs position weighting and pair blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision on the same target-generated responses. The auxiliary objective trains next-token prediction from unmasked response prefixes, adding distinct conditioning pattern to the masked-block training objective. Other methods optimize how candidate tokens are organized and selected for verification. DiffuSpec searches for causally consistent paths through parallel token predictions and adapts draft length using recent acceptance feedback [Li et al., 2026]. SpecDiff-2 selects among multiple sampled drafts using verifier-based criterion [Sandler et al., 2025]. DART and DDTree organize parallel predictions into candidate trees [Liu et al., 2026, Ringel and Romano, 2026], while CaDDTree jointly selects tree structure and node budget using throughput objective [Zhang et al., 2026c]. DSpark couples parallel backbone with lightweight sequential module and selects verification length using prefix acceptance estimates and serving load [Cheng et al., 2026]. These methods modify candidate dependencies or verification choices; D3D studies the training and layer redundancy of the underlying standalone diffusion drafter.

sections.title: 2.2 Layer Pruning for Efficient Drafting
sections.content: ShortGPT ranks layers by the similarity between their input and output representations [Men et al., 2025]. SDFP uses Fisher information to select layers for removal and constructs drafters without recovery training [Wei et al., 2026]. Yan et al. [2025a] study structured pruning for shallow draft architectures and show that language-model accuracy is poor predictor of speculative-decoding performance. D3D evaluates layer removal through its effect on acceptance length, directly measuring the retained models utility for block drafting. Self-data distillation restores quality after layer pruning using responses generated by the unpruned model [Thangarasa et al., 2025]. SD2 applies self-distillation to fine-grained sparse drafters and also evaluates layer-pruned alternatives [Lasby et al., 2025]. Our procedure alternates layer removal with recovery training and reassesses acceptance-based layer importance after recovery, so each pruning decision reflects the updated drafter. Within diffusion drafting, DFlare studies greater depth with layer-specific fusion of target features [Zhang et al., 2026a]; D3D studies depth reduction while retaining nearly all of trained standalone drafters acceptance length. 3 Figure 1: Overview of D3D. (a) Drafter training. Target-generated responses supervise blockwise denoising and auxiliary autoregressive prediction. Packed attention shares causal prefix computation while isolating diffusion blocks and allowing bidirectional attention within each block. (b) Progressive layer pruning. Each iteration removes the layer causing the smallest decrease in validation acceptance length, followed by recovery and reevaluation of layer importance. Recovery uses distillation from fixed unpruned drafter whose output distribution is adjusted toward the supervised token. (c) Asynchronous inference. During target verification, one packed drafter pass prepares successor blocks for alternative rejection outcomes and full acceptance. branch matching the verified prefix is reused; otherwise, the drafter generates new block synchronously.

sections.title: 2.3 Asynchronous Speculative Decoding
sections.content: PipeInfer maintains speculative execution during pipeline-parallel inference and cancels computation along invalid paths [Butler et al., 2024]. SwiftSpec separates drafting and verification across GPU groups and coordinates parallel tree generation with cache management [Zhang et al., 2025]. Speculative Speculative Decoding (SSD) caches follow-up drafts for possible verification outcomes and uses fallback strategy when the observed outcome has no cached draft [Kumar et al., 2026]. SSD explicitly accommodates different drafter architectures, including diffusion models. Inspired by SSD, D3D combines target-aligned drafter training and acceptance-guided pruning with packed successor prediction during target verification.

sections.title: 3.1 Overview
sections.content: D3D is standalone diffusion drafter Md for asynchronous speculative decoding with an autoregressive target model Mt. Conditioned on the token prefix, Md computes its own prefix representations and generates candidate block in single forward pass, without accessing target hidden states. The target verifies the 4 candidate tokens in parallel using rejection sampling and appends one additional token after the accepted prefix. Our objective is to fully hide drafting latency within target verification while maintaining long accepted prefixes. When drafting is fully hidden, target verification determines the ideal latency of each decoding round. We initialize Md from pretrained autoregressive model and train on target-generated responses using blockwise denoising and auxiliary autoregressive supervision (Section 3.2). We then exploit redundancy across drafter layers through acceptance-guided pruning to reduce drafting latency while preserving the trained drafters acceptance length (Section 3.3). Section 3.4 describes concurrent drafting and verification and the conditions for hiding drafting latency. Figure 1 summarizes the training, pruning, and inference stages.

sections.title: 3.2 Target-Aligned Drafter Training
sections.content: A standalone drafter must encode the token prefix and predict continuations using its own representations. We initialize Md from pretrained autoregressive model to use its learned language priors. For each prompt = (p1, . . . , pL), we generate response = (r1, . . . , rT ) using Mt and train Md on these response tokens.

sections.title: 3.3 Acceptance-Guided Layer Pruning
sections.content: (6) (7) We exploit redundancy across drafter layers to reduce drafting latency while preserving average acceptance length. With the target model and block size fixed, we measure validation acceptance length after separately removing each remaining layer (Figure 1(b)). We remove the single layer whose removal causes the smallest decrease in average acceptance length, then perform recovery training. Layer removal changes the inputs to subsequent layers, and recovery training updates the remaining parameters. We therefore recompute layer importance on the recovered model before the next pruning step. Recovery training uses knowledge distillation [Hinton et al., 2015] from the trained, unpruned drafter, which remains fixed throughout pruning. sections.title: Inference
sections.content: Mt generates the first response token as the initial anchor, and Md predicts 1 candidate tokens in single forward pass, forming block of size B. The target verifies these candidates in parallel using rejection sampling with their corresponding proposal probabilities [Leviathan et al., 2023]. It appends the accepted candidates and samples the next token from the residual distribution at the first rejection, or from the target distribution if all candidates are accepted. During verification, Md prepares continuations for possible verification outcomes in single packed forward pass (Figure 1(c)). Each rejection branch extends the existing output prefix with the candidates 6 preceding the rejection position, an alternative anchor, and predicted continuation. For full acceptance, the drafter also prepares continuation conditioned on the entire current block. cache hit occurs when the complete verified prefix, including the target-generated token, matches the initial token sequence of prepared branch. We reuse the remaining draft tokens of the matching branch for the next verification round. On cache miss, the target must wait for Md to synchronously generate new block from the verified prefix before the next verification round can begin. We define the cache hit rate phit as the probability of hit in verification round. Position coverage includes the first 1 rejection positions and the full-acceptance case. Token fanout is the number of alternative anchors per selected rejection position [Kumar et al., 2026]. We select the most probable tokens under the drafter distribution, excluding the proposed token; under greedy drafting, these have ranks 2, . . . , + 1. The packed input contains the current block which is being verified, (C 1)F blocks for rejection outcomes, and one block for full acceptance. With token positions per block, the asynchronous draft budget is Nasync = [(C 1)F + 2] . (11) Let td and tv denote the latencies of packed drafting and target verification under concurrent execution. For stages that begin simultaneously, cache hit hides the packed drafting latency when td tv. Larger budgets can increase td and reduce the latency benefit obtained from higher cache-hit rate. Acceptanceguided pruning aims to reduce td with minimal loss in acceptance length.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Models and Evaluation We evaluate D3D with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B as target models across seven benchmarks. These cover mathematical reasoning (GSM8K, MATH-500, and AIME25), code generation (HumanEval, MBPP, and LiveCodeBench-v6), and open-ended dialogue (MT-Bench). We report decoding speedup relative to autoregressive decoding and average acceptance length τ . We define τ as the mean number of output tokens added per verification round, including the token generated by the target model. Training Data We use prompts from Open-PerfectBlend, an instruction-tuning dataset containing 1.42 million examples. We regenerate responses with the corresponding target model in non-thinking mode, using its recommended sampling settings. Baselines We compare D3D with DFlash [Chen et al., 2026], DSpark [Cheng et al., 2026], EAGLE-3 [Li et al., 2025], PARD-2 [An et al., 2026], and SSD [Kumar et al., 2026]. PARD-2 and SSD are evaluated using asynchronous inference. For Qwen3-8B, we use the public DSpark and EAGLE-3 checkpoints released by the DSpark authors, both trained on Open-PerfectBlend. We train DFlash and PARD-2 for both targets, and DSpark and EAGLE-3 for Qwen3-32B, on the same target-generated training data as D3D. Implementation The main experiments use D3D-8B, initialized from Qwen3-8B and progressively pruned from 36 to 31 Transformer layers, with = 16, = 12, and = 2 for both targets (Section 3.4). Targetaligned drafter training uses 128 random anchors per example and 3 training epochs (360 GPU hours). Target-aligned drafter training and recovery training use BF16 on two NVIDIA H800 GPUs with 8-bit AdamW. We use local batch size of 1 and gradient accumulation steps of 8, giving global batch size of 16. We use cosine learning-rate schedule from 105 to 106 with 1% warmup, zero weight decay, and gradient-norm clipping at 1. 7 For pruning, we reuse the target-aligned training data and perform 10k recovery training steps per stage. Layer selection and checkpoint selection are performed on two separate, non-overlapping development sets, with acceptance length evaluated on 512 examples per set. All evaluations use the Transformers backend with greedy decoding in non-thinking mode. D3D, SSD, and PARD-2 use two H800 GPUs; the synchronous DFlash, DSpark, and EAGLE-3 baselines run on one.

sections.title: 4.3 Ablation Studies
sections.content: Auxiliary autoregressive supervision. We assess the contribution of auxiliary AR supervision by varying λ in Eq. (7) and training each D3D-1.7B variant for one epoch (Table 3, left). Setting λ = 1 increases τ by 0.24 to 0.40 tokens over diffusion-only training (λ = 0) across all four benchmarks; increasing λ to 1.5 provides no further improvement. The GSM8K training curves show that the benefit persists throughout training (Appendix B.1). Blockwise denoising trains parallel predictions, while the AR objective continues to supervise next-token prediction from unmasked prefixes. This supervision helps the standalone drafter learn to predict from its own prefix representations without target hidden states. We therefore use λ = 1 during target-aligned drafter training. Drafter scale. The scale ablation examines whether D3Ds acceptance advantage requires larger parameter budget. We train its 1.7B, 4B, and 8B variants for one epoch and compare them with DFlash (Table 3, right). D3D-1.7B achieves higher acceptance than DFlash on all three benchmarks with fewer total parameters (2.0B versus 2.3B). On MATH-500, increasing drafter size from 1.7B to 4B improves τ by 1.29 tokens, while increasing it from 4B to 8B adds 0.44 tokens; HumanEval and MT-Bench show similar diminishing gains. The AR and initialization ablations separately show that both training choices improve acceptance at fixed architecture. The smaller gains at larger scales motivate pruning the trained 8B drafter to reduce drafting cost while retaining its acceptance. To test whether depth reduction improves speedup with little loss in acceptance, we evaluate progressively pruned and recovered D3D-8B checkpoints under asynchronous inference (Figure 2, left). Pruning from 36 to 31 layers reduces depth by 13.9% while retaining over 99% of mean τ across MATH-500, HumanEval, and MT-Bench. The 31-layer checkpoint achieves the highest mean decoding speedup among the tested depths, at 4.69. The small acceptance loss indicates that part of the original depth is redundant for drafting after recovery. Reducing drafting work makes it easier to overlap drafting with verification, while the retained acceptance keeps the average number of output tokens per round nearly unchanged. Below 31 layers, acceptance length and speedup both decline, indicating that further computational savings no longer compensate for the loss in draft quality. We therefore select the final recovered checkpoint by validation decoding speedup. Pretrained initialization. Holding the drafter architecture and training budget fixed, we compare Qwen38B weights with random initialization to isolate the contribution of pretraining (Figure 2, right). At the final measured training step, pretrained initialization yields τ 9.8 on GSM8K, compared with τ 4.5 for random initialization; the advantage emerges early and persists throughout training. pretrained model already predicts plausible continuations from token prefix, allowing adaptation to focus on target alignment and parallel block prediction. randomly initialized drafter must also learn this prediction capability within the same training budget. Asynchronous draft budget. Two sweeps examine the tradeoff between speculative coverage and drafting cost: varying position coverage at fixed = 2, and varying token fan-out at fixed = 12 (Figure 3). We use the 31-layer D3D-8B drafter on AIME25. Both sweeps achieve their highest speedup of approximately 5.0 at = 12, = 2, and 384-token asynchronous draft budget. Increasing from 12 to 16 at = 2 raises the hit rate from 71.3% to 78.3% but reduces speedup. At = 12, increasing from 2 to 5 raises the hit rate to 81.8% and the budget to 912 tokens, with lower speedup than at = 2. Cache hits avoid new drafting pass after verification, reducing the delay before the next round. Increasing coverage adds computation to every packed drafting pass, including branches that verification never selects. We therefore select the budget by decoding speedup to account for cache reuse and the cost of preparing successor blocks. Right: varying token fan-out at = 12.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented D3D, which provides the first empirical demonstration of asynchronous lossless speculative decoding with standalone diffusion drafter. Target-aligned training combines blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision to adapt pretrained model for single-pass block prediction without target hidden states. Acceptance-guided progressive pruning with recovery training reduces drafting latency with little loss in acceptance length. Across seven benchmarks, D3D achieves average decoding speedups of 5.00 and 5.71 over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B as targets, respectively. These average speedups exceed those of both SSD and asynchronously deployed PARD-2 in our evaluation. With Qwen3-8B as the target, pruning D3D-8B from 36 to 31 layers retains over 99% of the unpruned drafters mean acceptance length across three benchmarks. These results show that target-aligned training and acceptance-guided pruning make standalone diffusion drafting effective for asynchronous lossless speculative decoding.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: We evaluate D3D, SSD, and PARD-2 with one GPU for the target and another for the drafter. The drafter adds model memory and speculative computation. We have not compared throughput per GPU against alternative uses of the same two-GPU budget, such as target inference using tensor parallelism. Cache misses require synchronous drafting before verification can resume. Our implementation uses Transformers; evaluating D3D in production frameworks such as SGLang or vLLM with their batching and scheduling optimizations remains future work.

sections.title: B Additional Ablations
sections.content: B.1 Training Dynamics We examine whether auxiliary AR supervision provides sustained benefit by tracking GSM8K acceptance length during one-epoch D3D-1.7B training (Figure 4). After the initial training phase, nonzero AR weights yield higher acceptance than diffusion-only training (λ = 0). Among the tested weights, λ = 1 generally gives the highest acceptance; increasing it to 1.5 provides no further benefit. The sustained advantage supports maintaining next-token supervision during diffusion adaptation, where it continues to constrain predictions from unmasked prefixes. Figure 4: GSM8K acceptance length τ during D3D-1.7B training with different auxiliary autoregressive loss weights λ. The target is Qwen3-8B and the block size is = 16. 15 B.2 Block Size To examine how block size affects acceptance and decoding speedup, we train separate D3D-8B drafters for one epoch at {8, 16, 32}. We evaluate each drafter at its training block size under asynchronous Increasing from 8 to 16 improves speedup on MATH-500 and inference with Qwen3-8B  (Table 4)  . HumanEval, while MT-Bench is slightly faster at = 8. Increasing further to 32 raises acceptance length but reduces speedup on all three tasks; on MATH-500, τ increases from 9.89 to 12.39 while speedup falls from 5.55 to 3.16. Larger blocks permit longer accepted prefixes but also add candidate positions for drafting and verification, including tokens that verification may discard. We use = 16 as the default because it achieves the highest mean speedup across the three tasks. Table 4: Decoding speedup and acceptance length τ versus block size; D3D-8B, Qwen3-8B target. 8 16 32 MATH-500 HumanEval MT-Bench Speedup τ Speedup τ Speedup τ 4.58 6.26 5.55 9.89 3.16 12.39 4.00 5.52 4.47 7.85 2.56 8.70 2.55 4.38 2.47 5.72 1.42 6.33 B.3 Number of Training Anchors The number of sampled anchors controls how many diffusion blocks each response contributes to training. We test whether denser supervision improves acceptance by training D3D-1.7B for one epoch with {16, 64, 128, 256} anchors per response, using Qwen3-8B as the target and = 16  (Table 5)  . Increasing from 16 to 64 improves τ by 0.25, 0.21, and 0.04 tokens on MATH-500, HumanEval, and MT-Bench, respectively. Increasing from 64 to 256 adds only 0.03, 0.03, and 0.06 tokens. Given that target-generated responses average fewer than 2,048 tokens, the limited gains suggest that = 128 at = 16 already provides sufficient supervision across response positions. Doubling adds more overlapping blocks and training computation, but improves acceptance length by at most 0.02 tokens on each task. We therefore use = 128. MATH-500 HumanEval MT-Bench 16 64 128 256 7.89 8.14 8.15 8.17 6.00 6.21 6.24 6.24 4.41 4.45 4.50 4.51 Selective Prefilling with D3D Our main results use trained standalone diffusion drafter for full-prompt asynchronous speculative decoding. For each drafter size, we use single trained checkpoint for both prompt selection and sequential speculative decoding. Prefilling fewer tokens reduces target computation and can further improve endto-end latency. Because the target conditions on reduced prompt, we report task scores alongside latency 16 speedups to quantify the qualitylatency trade-off. Decoding remains target-verified for the retained prompt. SpecPrefill [Liu et al., 2025] suggests reusing its token selector for speculative decoding but provides no experimental results for the combination. To our knowledge, this is the first long-context evaluation in which standalone diffusion drafter performs both prompt selection and speculative drafting. Figure 5: Selective prefilling and sequential speculative decoding with D3D. The same standalone drafter scores prompt chunks for target prefilling and generates candidate blocks for verification. Retained chunks preserve their original order, and the drafter and target maintain separate KV caches. Inference setting. Figure 5 illustrates the inference workflow. For prompt = (x1, . . . , xL), we run the standalone drafter on the full prompt and score prompt chunks with one-MASK importance probe. Given target retention fraction ρ {0.1, 0.2, 0.3}, we select the highest-scoring chunks to retain approximately ρL tokens, preserving their original order to obtain xρ. The target model prefills xρ; the same drafter then prepares blocks of size 16 (one target anchor and 15 drafted tokens) for sequential, target-verified speculative decoding. The drafter maintains its own prefix cache, separate from the target cache built on xρ. Greedy verification follows the target model conditioned on xρ; selecting xρ can change the output relative to conditioning on the original prompt x. Evaluation. We evaluate Qwen3-32B on 18 datasets across five task categories from the original LongBench [Bai et al., 2024]. We compare full-prompt sequential D3D drafting with selective-prefill variants retaining 10%, 20%, or 30% of the prompt. Tables 6 and 7 report the LongBench score for each category and the speedup in time to first token (TTFT), decoding, and end-to-end (E2E) latency relative to full-prompt AR decoding in the same category. Full denotes the complete prompt; percentages denote the target retention fraction. Higher is better in every column. TTFT speedups therefore fall below 1 despite faster decoding. Selective prefilling adds substantial end-to-end gains to D3Ds decoding acceleration. With the 8B drafter, 30% retention improves E2E speedup over Full + D3D in all five LongBench categories, spanning document QA, summarization, few-shot learning, and code completion, while keeping scores close to full-prompt results. The gains persist at lower retention: on single-document QA, 10% raises E2E speedup from 1.40 to 3.32 with score of 47.05 versus 47.91 for Full + D3D; at 20%, multi-document QA scores 46.95 at 2.59 E2E speedup. The same trained standalone drafter thus accelerates target prefilling and decoding across tasks and retention levels. Drafter size. larger drafter improves QA under aggressive selective prefilling. At 10% retention, the 8B drafter scores 47.05 on single-document QA versus 41.27 for the 1.7B drafter; both score 47.91 with the full prompt. The gap appears when the drafter selects the targets context, indicating that larger capacity helps preserve the information needed for accurate answers with much shorter target prompt. Prompt retention. smaller target prompt can add to the E2E gain from speculative drafting. On multidocument QA with the 8B drafter, retaining 20% of the prompt scores 46.95 versus 45.97 with Full + D3D, and increases E2E speedup from 1.54 to 2.59. Selection reduces the targets prefill work while keeping the context needed for answering; the same drafter continues to accelerate decoding. Speedup across tasks. The balance between prefilling and decoding determines how much decoding acceleration translates into E2E speedup. With the 8B drafter at 30% retention, summarization reaches 3.37 E2E speedup, close to its 3.48 decoding speedup. Single-document QA reaches 2.62 E2E despite 5.49 faster decoding. Summarization spends more of its runtime generating the response, while prefilling accounts for larger share in QA. Accelerating both stages yields substantial E2E gains across these different task profiles.
